I just fresh installed the `RPC-handler` package and used `ctrl + f` to detect which rpcs and explorers are in the current build via `index.js` using that list you linked.
---
If we were to add our own endpoints that we host or something then it might make sense but public endpoints are pretty much covered and I'd say this task can be closed. 
I'm unaware of the package bugging out and not finding a provider but if a task was opened regarding it I'd be happy to investigate.
This should be impossible for the top chains that most use but once we start to deal with less popular chains then it's possible it could but we'd never be able to host whitelisted rpcs for all chains anyway.

I can't say I experienced this personally while building/stabilising the test suites while I was `pay.ubq.fi`'s maintainer. I'm assuming this edge-case only exists in the test suite and it hasn't been a problem in a prod setting?
First of all, `pay.ubq.fi` test env extracts an RPC and then tries to init `Anvil.fork(rpc)` so it does not benefit from retry-reselect which anybody using `rpc-handler` in production would benefit from.
`Anvil.Fork` is a vm essentially and is prone to weird errors within it's infra - see https://www.github.com/foundry-rs/foundry/issues/4082 as one example.
It seems that OS can play into things and I'm a Windows dweeb, which may be why I never experienced it?
Although based on the video (which btw ty) I can make educated guesses.
1. The logic for `rpc-handler` largely remains untouched so I'm inclined to believe at first that it's an Anvil or RPC-specific issue.
2. Based on the error given `Fork Error.. "invalid number"` - I'd begin debugging there, starting with using the RPCs which bugged out and running them n times to see how often they fail. I'd then see if changing the numbers either in terms of value or how they are fed as input (E.G. hex/dec) makes a difference. It's a pretty shit error message but maybe it's talking about a number unrelated to the payload we provide and it's something anvil is inserting for gas for example.
3. Potentially a `cache` issue that's causing it, again on the Anvil side.
4. The fact it succeeds against RPC-A and fails against RPC-B with the same payload, could be that the RPC API is different in some way (which does happen, most commonly with methods tho not input schema).
The fact that `rpc-handler` successful performed it's health-check against those RPC and it was deemed the fastest to respond followed by Anvil's failure to execute a forked tx, I'd lean on it being Anvil more so than `rpc-handler`. Ofc I'm basically stabbing in the dark without looking into things properly.
If needed, open a task and tag me and I'll look into things, happy to help.

Which of the below options is the spec implying?
A) `rpc-handler` was not able to find a _singular_ provider for a specific network as-in no suitable providers were found post-health check?
B) A read/write op failed with the given provider(s) and we'd like to fallback to "official" ones in the case where the op failed?
The code reads like A, `rpc-handler` could not find even one provider for that network.
In either case, I think your example @EresDev (without knowledge of it happening through intended usage of `rpc-handler`) doesn't quite apply due to the fact we extract the `RPC` and then the error happens within `Anvil`. I could be wrong tho it would need debugged specifically for me to know for sure.

Again, the problem by my estimation lies with Anvil, not `rpc-handler`. 
Any "official" RPCs that you guys add, are already inside `rpc-handler`.  The problem presented by @EresDev is detached from the `rpc-handler`'s main logic because we extract the RPC URL to init anvil with it, so no retry or reselect.

The reason `rpc-handler` was built was to avoid building a `blacklist` of RPCs that didn't work (for `pay.ubq.fi`), so to me we should avoid manually marking providers if we can.
It's still unclear what the problem question is:
1. `rpc-handler` could not find any providers? The footage shows providers returned successfully.
2. `rpc-handler` fails to handle tx failures? The footage does not have retry-reselect logic and was relying on Anvil internals to fake broadcast txs.
Difficult for us to determine sync but maybe we can use the majority value of `blocknumbers` and eliminate outliers that way?
You made a comment which sort of attests to the fact even our whitelisted rpcs might fail for some, it feels like a losing battle.
---
Also it appears that the "fallback" logic was leftover and not removed once they got a hang of using `rpc-handler` within `allowance.ubq.fi` so I'm assuming that can be removed (I briefly scanned the commits).
---
Great idea yeah. I'm confident that in a production setting without Anvil, your retry-reselect logic will kick in and your tx will go through.
It's still unconfirmed if anyone has spotted issues in a prod setting, so my opinion is based on the fact there has been none.

1. Sync we can semi-estimate comparing `blocknumbers` I'd think, ofc it relies on a given network having a surplus of providers and the majority being in sync.
2. I'd expect the initial health-check to fail in such a case but either way the expectation of `rpc-handler` would be to activate it's internal retry-reselect logic I'd think. Perhaps it should be looked at if it's failing in those cases.
3. That's tricky. I guess we could `best out of three` for each provider? Pros and cons with this idk if it's optimal for the likes of ETH with 15+ providers etc.
We could call `_getBlock` to eliminate outliers then use an "expensive" read with an immutable return value to further knockout any that might hang, something like `permit2` or whatever comes to mind.
Where did we land on things then since this is priced and ready to go?

I just realized it's `Priority: 3 (High)` so I'm excluded from this task actually lmao. 
The task access is pretty grim rn, especially with marketing contacting hundreds of devs as we speak. Any that are decent will be restricted to menial tasks which won't excite them to partake. 
I know it was a temp fix to stop the team from being overloaded by sub-par PRs from new contributors but maybe things need reviewed a bit.

comments.content: @Keyrxng Pls check the description and confirm if it's relevant

Overall there're at least 2 repos ([one](https://github.com/ubiquity/permit2-allowance.ubq.fi/blob/04587e0f5324e794e587b9ee59a8246984c4d00f/static/constants.ts), [two](https://github.com/ubiquity/pay.ubq.fi/blob/d0a31486cfc3ebe0bf122dc511a9c5a71cedb6fb/shared/use-rpc-handler.ts#L48)) that use their own RPCs in case `rpc-handler` fails which is not a good sign. As far as I understand `rpc-handler` works this way: 1. Fetch RPCs from https://chainid.network/chains.json for a given network 2. Send `eth_getBlockByNumber` for each RPC and measure latency 3. Return RPC with the lowest latency The thing is that any latency <500ms looks good for an end user so this parameter is important but not the most crucial one. What's more important is the correct latest block number which means that RPC node is in sync with the latest state. Check this screenshot which highlights RPC with low latency but wrong latest block number: So the fastest RPC may not be reliable in the end (for example I regularly have issues with https://eth.drpc.org RPC). We've already discarded the following options: 1. Use self-hosted RPC node (had issues with cloudflare setup) 2. Use private RPC nodes from alchemy or similar services (have to expose API keys in the frontend) We could mark certain RPC nodes as "stable". I mean that I personally sure that `https://eth.llamarpc.com` is a pretty stable choice for mainnet while `https://rpc.gnosischain.com` is stable for gnosis chain although their latencies may not be the fastest. We could change the sorting algorithm of `rpc-handler` to: 1. Send `eth_getBlockByNumber` for each "stable" RPC and measure latency 2. If there is at least 1 live "stable" RPC then return it 3. Fetch RPCs from https://chainid.network/chains.json for a given network (excluding "stable" RPCs from that list) 4. Send `eth_getBlockByNumber` for each "unstable" RPC and measure latency 5. Simply return RPC with the lowest latency

`rpc-handler` may return RPC node which is:
- out of sync (i.e. not on the latest block) 
- not accessible for the end user (like https://eth.llamarpc.com for me which works only via VPN)
- not reliable like `https://eth.drpc.org` (which responds to `eth_getBlock` but hangs for further requests which [causes](https://github.com/ubiquity-os-marketplace/text-conversation-rewards/actions/runs/13383655396/job/37376464060) `text-conversation-rewards` plugin to compute rewards for ~15 minutes instead of 15 seconds)
I've removed fallback to a whitelisted RPC from the issue description. Now it simply describes 3 `rpc-handler` issues that should be solved.

`rpc-handler` may return RPC node which is:
- out of sync (i.e.     not on the latest block) 
- not accessible for the end user (like https://eth.llamarpc.com for me which works only via VPN)
- not reliable like `https://eth.drpc.org` (which responds to `eth_getBlock` but hangs for further requests which [causes](https://github.com/ubiquity-os-marketplace/text-conversation-rewards/actions/runs/13383655396/job/37376464060) `text-conversation-rewards` plugin to compute rewards for ~15 minutes instead of 15 seconds)
As a part of this task we should fix all of the above issues.

To sum up `rpc-handler` now works this way:
1. Fetch RPCs from https://chainid.network/chains.json for a given network
2. Send `eth_getBlockByNumber` and `eth_getCode` (to fetch permit2 smart contract bytecode) for each RPC and measure latency
3. Find most common block and exclude RPCs out of sync (even if difference is 1 block)
4. Return RPC with the lowest latency and with the most common block
Regarding the issues mentioned in the original task description:
- out of sync, not on the latest block (now `rpc-handler` compares block heights for RPCs)
- not accessible for the end user, like https://eth.llamarpc.com/ for me which works only via VPN (in this case `rpc-handler` simply won't return the RPC as operational since it wouldn't be able to measure latency)
- not reliable like https://eth.drpc.org which responds to `eth_getBlock` but hangs for further requests (now `rpc-handler` also reads the state, in particular tries to fetch permit2 bytecode)

- Using rpc-handler's rpc: tests passed: 1/4 times. 25% success rate

- can we improve this when running tests? 
```
A worker process has failed to exit gracefully and has been force exited. This is likely caused by tests leaking due to improper teardown. Try running with --detectOpenHandles to find leaks. Active timers can also cause this, ensure that .unref() was called on them.
```

Some info to improve the code quality. You don't need to do this now but something useful to consider for the future I think.
- naming needs improvement. we should reduce the use of terms like Service, Handler, Managers. These are too generic. Name of class or function should indicate clear intent and should follow Single Responsibility Principle.
- if all functions were going to be static, then use functions instead of class I think. Even though I believe class would be more useful but with minimum statics. This will enable inheritance and we can offer more to users like class FastestRpc, AnonymousRpc, SecureRpc that can inherit from class AnyRpc.
- use immutability. do not change objects passed in arguments to functions. Clone them if you must before changing, and return them from function. A function should almost never change an object pass in arguments. This can introduce hard to debug problems.
